abstract: This paper investigates the actual online consumption of political misinformation during the 2016 US presidential campaign, addressing gaps in knowledge about the volume, slant, and behavioral effects of exposure to factually dubious 'fake news' websites. Combining survey data with web-traffic data, the authors examine who was exposed to untrustworthy websites, the role of social media and fact checking in driving exposure, and downstream behavioral effects. The findings indicate that supporters of Donald Trump were disproportionately exposed to such content.
key_claims: Little empirical knowledge exists about the actual volume and slant of political misinformation consumed online, despite widespread concern about echo chambers.
Exposure to untrustworthy ('fake news') websites during the 2016 campaign was concentrated among specific segments of the electorate rather than evenly distributed.
Trump supporters were disproportionately exposed to factually dubious content.
methods: Analysis combining survey data with individual-level web-traffic (browsing) data collected during the 2016 US presidential campaign.
Operationalizing 'fake news' as exposure to websites that publish factually dubious content.
Examining the role of social media referrals and fact checking in shaping exposure patterns.
findings: Supporters of Donald Trump exhibited higher exposure to untrustworthy websites during the 2016 campaign (full detail truncated in available abstract).
Exposure to political misinformation was unevenly distributed across the electorate.
The study assesses—but the abstract does not fully report—the effects of social media and fact checking on exposure and the behavioral consequences of misinformation.
contributions: Provides empirical measurement of the actual volume and slant of online political misinformation consumption rather than relying on speculation about echo chambers.
Links behavioral web-traffic data to survey responses to characterize who consumes fake news.
Advances understanding of the roles of social media and fact checking in exposure to misinformation.
framing: The paper situates itself within debates over online misinformation, echo chambers, and 'fake news' in political communication, seeking to replace commentary-driven assumptions with empirical evidence on actual consumption patterns during a major election.
